prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my sole part and I have not changed configuration since round 1. The chair asks what the clock gives us beyond accuracy. My answer is that it is now a laboratory instrument that reads a gravitational potential across a millimetre, that constrains drifts of fundamental constants, and that sets limits on dark-matter couplings. Those are clues from nature, which is the test I apply to any elegant idea, and here the clues come from experiment. The idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping) is simple, the performance (Ye's group at the 1e-18 level) was demonstrated, and the result has been reproduced and surpassed independently at several national laboratories. That is the combination I trust. The credit chain is short, with two people and no collaboration of hundreds. The 2005 prize recognised the comb and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems; neither recognised trapping a very large ensemble of neutral atoms with the trap removed from the measurement, and that is a distinct step in principle. Timing is good, and I do not think the formal redefinition of the second needs to come first, since the performance is already confirmed.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is still that this is an invention and measurement capability, and our own emphasis is that discoveries come first and people second. A sceptic can say that the physics payoff (redshift tests, constants, dark matter) has so far confirmed what we expected and has not delivered a surprise. The clock stands on the comb and on laser cooling, both already honoured. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and I cannot make that gap disappear with wording. I think a citation can honour the invention without claiming exclusivity, but I accept that some will read the omission as unfair. Finally, if the committee decided to wait for the redefinition of the second, I could not claim that the clock would lose standing by waiting a year.

responses.point: Lindroth, as an atomic theorist, says the physics stands on its own: the light-shift theory behind the magic wavelength is well understood, calculation and experiment agree, and the result opens questions about constants and time in a gravitational potential. She also flags the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the strongest reservation.
responses.response: This is the answer I wanted from an atomic physicist, because I am a string theorist and cannot judge the light-shift details myself. I read her point that agreement between calculation and experiment is what the field depends on as the reason the clock is a measurement of nature and not only a machine. On overlap I land where she does: the comb and ion control are tools the clock uses, but the magic-wavelength principle is a new idea that neither prize contains. I would ask her whether she is comfortable with a citation that names the invention and states the 10^-18 level, because that wording, not a longer list of names, is how we honour the other groups without pretending they are absent.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new class of quantum matter, confirmed over fifteen years and arguably overdue, and defers to the atomic physicists on whether the lattice clock is a discovery.
responses.response: I take his case seriously, since it is the strongest conceptual argument on the list and the physics is a discovery in the plainest sense. My problem is credit, and I do not see it resolved in this round. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction guided the HgTe experiment and sits outside the trio, Shoucheng Zhang is no longer alive to be added, and the 3D and ARPES work is only partly covered. A citation built on 'prediction and first observation' implicitly says that the trio is the right cut, and I do not believe that is certain. The 2016 prize is a smaller worry for me than the credit gap. I keep B007 as my first alternative, and if the committee were to find a clean wording I would not oppose it in a later year, but I will not move it ahead of a case with a short and consistent credit chain.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators and says candidly that he is the member most predisposed to the theory side of that field, so he should discount his own enthusiasm. He ranks the clock second and does not oppose it.
responses.response: I respect that discount and I would apply the same discipline to myself: I am also a theorist, and I would be tempted by a conceptually clean mechanism over an instrument. That is exactly why I tried in round 1 to ask what the clock tells us about nature. His point that the Z2 mechanism is simple and general is correct, but simplicity of the mechanism does not repair the question of who is named. Since he lists B056 as his alternative and says he would not oppose a later year for B007, I think we may be closer than the counts suggest, and the real question for him is whether the BHZ gap is a reason to wait or only a footnote.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved B056 from fifth to first on the grounds of independent confirmation and instrument performance, asks for a citation that honours the lattice clock as a distinct invention, and notes that his first-place IceCube vote came from closeness to his own field.
responses.response: I agree with his test, and his candour about field closeness is useful. On IceCube, which he and I both keep as an alternative, my round-1 question stands: AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal, and a collaboration of that size, make a two-name credit for Halzen and Karle more contestable than for the clock, and source identification is at the evidence level. I would be glad to be corrected by him on whether the diffuse flux alone, confirmed in several channels, is a sufficient discovery for this year. If it is, then the attribution question is the only thing left, and I do not think we can settle that in the next few days. For the citation, I propose we name the invention and its performance, as in my line above, and add nothing about parallel groups.

responses.point: Kroll states that the 2005 and 2012 prizes make a continuation argument possible but does not find the wait-for-redefinition argument compelling, since performance is confirmed by JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, with clock-to-clock fibre-link comparisons routine.
responses.response: I agree that waiting would add little. A redefinition is a decision of the metrology community, and the physics case does not depend on it. What I would add is that his clock-to-clock comparisons are the strongest answer to the discovery-versus-invention worry: when several independent laboratories compare to 1e-18 and the numbers agree, that is verification by nature and not by a single lab. I would drop atom interferometry as the second pillar for the reason I gave in round 1, namely overlap among Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich with Chu honoured in 1997, so I do not see a case for a two-part configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept an invention and measurement capability as a discovery in the Nobel sense, and whether the redshift, constants and dark-matter results carry enough weight to make that case.
Whether the omission of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams is defensible with Katori and Ye alone, and whether the citation wording can avoid implying exclusivity.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap in B007 can be closed by a citation, or whether it should postpone the topological-insulator prize.
Whether the IceCube diffuse-flux discovery is mature enough, and whether the two-name credit for Halzen and Karle can survive the AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal lineage.
Whether the 2016 topology prize and the 2025 circuits prize change the timing of the competing candidates.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. None of Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or the IceCube names is a supervisor, close collaborator or Uppsala colleague. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are unrelated to the shortlisted candidates. I am a string theorist and not an atomic physicist, so on the fine points of the clock I rely on Lindroth and Kroll.
